article: Does “results may vary” explain what a skincare buyer should expect?
Read the FTC’s approach to exceptional testimonials and distinguish an individual story from a typical result.
U.S. Federal Trade Commission endorsement guidance. Explains how to interpret testimonial wording.
copy: A personal testimonial describes one experience. Under FTC guidance, an endorsement showing an exceptional outcome can imply that consumers generally can expect it. A generic statement that results vary does not tell the reader what the expected result is.
Ask what the advertiser knows about the usual result

Start by separating the example from the supporting evidence. Look for a defined outcome in a representative group and a description of what happened under comparable circumstances. A truthful story can still be an unusual one. If an ad provides no evidence about ordinary experience, the expected effect remains unclear.
Keep the disclosure and the size of the claimed effect separate when reading the ad.

article: Can a filter be unrelated to a cosmetics claim?
Use UK advertising guidance to distinguish a photo edit from an edit that changes the exact feature the ad promises.
UK CAP advertising guidance on cosmetic production techniques. Examples are hypothetical.
copy: Editing a background and editing the lash volume in a mascara ad are different actions. UK advertising guidance focuses on whether a technique exaggerates the performance that the ad claims. The appearance of the feature being sold matters more than whether any styling occurred at all.
Look at what the ad asks you to believe

Read the language next to the image. If it claims longer-looking lashes, an edit that lengthens those lashes changes the evidence the viewer sees. A caption about the setup may help describe the photo, but the image still needs to represent the claimed outcome honestly.
If the claim depends on a comparison image, look for evidence that matches the actual advertised feature and product.
table: Did it leave the relevant feature comparable?
Did it exaggerate the advertised result?

article: Does an edited-photo warning have the same effect as showing a different image?
Read an original image-label experiment by its independent image and disclosure conditions.
Original studies of edited-image disclosures and appearance outcomes in specified groups.
copy: An image warning and the image itself are two different exposures. One original experiment distinguished whether photos were digitally modified and whether a warning appeared. That design makes it possible to ask different questions about the picture, the disclosure and their combination.
Identify what changed in each test condition

If a study changes both the image and the label at once, its result cannot cleanly isolate the effect of either change. Also check that the measured outcome matches the headline. A brief body-satisfaction rating is a specific immediate response, rather than a measure of every viewer’s long-term experience.
Use the actual comparison groups when describing the study. An edited label does not undo the underlying change to the photograph.

article: Does a “fitspiration” study measure workouts or how people felt about working out?
Read the outcome in a study of athletes and non-athletes instead of treating motivation as observed exercise.
Original comparison of viewing fitspiration in female NCAA athletes and non-athletes.
copy: The original fitspiration experiment in athletes and non-athletes examined outcomes such as body dissatisfaction and exercise motivation after viewing content. A motivation rating is meaningful in that design, but it does not directly show how many workouts the participants completed over the following weeks.
Find the exact behavior the researchers tracked

A study could also count actual sessions, measure time spent exercising, or ask people to rate the strength of their intention. These outcomes need separate results. Participant background matters because trained athletes and people outside organized sport can respond differently.
Read what the investigators observed before treating a social post as evidence about exercise behavior.
table: Three outcomes that may appear under motivation
What participants said they intended to do
What participants actually did if tracked
How participants reported feeling about appearance

article: Why can two skin oil measurements disagree on the same face?
Read facial sebum studies by the measured site and keep forehead and cheek readings separate.
Original facial biophysical mapping and sebum measurement research. No diagnosis.
copy: Sebum is the oily material on the skin surface, and its measured amount varies across facial regions. Facial mapping studies therefore record sites such as the forehead and cheek rather than treating a single patch as a uniform measure of the whole face.
The measurement location belongs beside the number

If a before-and-after claim uses a forehead reading first and a cheek reading later, part of that difference could come from the site. Keep the reading area, instrument and preparation consistent. Recent washing and the amount of time before sampling are also useful details. A lower single reading does not establish a long-term result.
Report the sites separately when a study gives both. That preserves the comparison the instrument actually made.
table: Forehead, cheek or another named site

article: What does comparing identical twins control in a facial-aging study?
Read a study of twins with different smoking histories and distinguish shared background from random assignment.
Original observational identical-twin facial-aging research. No inference to individual exposure or treatment.
copy: Comparing identical twins helps account for genetic differences and some shared background. Original studies used pairs with different smoking histories to examine differences in facial signs. The study design did not randomly assign people to smoke or make their other lifetime exposures identical.
A paired comparison solves only some differences

Look at the reported assessment and which twin pairs were included. Sun exposure, occupations and routines can still differ, and the faces were assessed under the study’s chosen methods. The design offers a narrower comparison than unrelated photographs and still does not turn a specific visual feature into evidence about one person’s history.
Summarize the reported pair differences together with their scope.

article: Does “listed with the FDA” mean the agency approved a cosmetic?
Distinguish a facility registration, a cosmetic product listing and an approval claim.
U.S. FDA information on MoCRA cosmetics registration, listing and agency authority. Check actual category before interpreting claims.
copy: A U.S. cosmetic facility registration or product listing is a regulatory filing. It does not show that the agency reviewed a finished cosmetic and found it effective. Cosmetics generally do not require FDA premarket approval, with important category-specific exceptions such as most color additives.
Read the exact filing that the company names

If a product carries claims about treating a condition, the intended use can raise a different regulatory question. The filing described in an ad does not establish that those claims were evaluated. Look for the actual FDA record or category before treating a logo or registration number as external review.
Keep the company’s filing and the evidence supporting the advertised effect separate.

article: Is “hypoallergenic” a standardized safety rating on U.S. cosmetics?
Use FDA guidance to check what the label does and does not establish about a product.
FDA U.S. consumer guidance about cosmetic claims and ingredient information.
copy: The FDA says there is no federal standard or definition governing the term hypoallergenic on U.S. cosmetics. The word by itself therefore does not reveal a test method, which people were studied, or how an individual will react.
Identify the tested result and the ingredients

If the product also says it tested for a particular outcome, read what was measured. Ingredient information can answer a different question, such as whether the product names something you already know you need to avoid. The front label cannot replace the full ingredient list or clinical advice for known sensitivities.
If there is no comparable study or clear test description, leave the risk comparison unresolved.
table: Read the evidence behind the label

A result that needs its method and population
Formulation information relevant to a specific product

article: What can “not tested on animals” cover on a cosmetics label?
Check whether the statement applies to the finished product, its ingredients or suppliers.
U.S. FDA discussion of animal-testing claim scope for cosmetics.
copy: A company can use a phrase such as cruelty-free for different scopes. The FDA notes that the terms do not have legal definitions for this purpose in the U.S. A statement about a finished product may leave out how a supplier tested an ingredient or older information used in development.
Find the part of the supply chain the claim covers

Look for whose policy is described, the product or ingredients it covers and whether there is a named external standard. If a logo is relevant, check its own definition and current listing. The phrase alone is not evidence about a product’s effectiveness or a clinical outcome.
For comparisons, quote the actual policy scope. Avoid assuming a company-wide promise when a statement only names one finished item.

article: What does an organic cosmetics label certify about the ingredients?
Read FDA and USDA labeling context before treating an agricultural claim as a safety or performance result.
FDA and USDA U.S. labeling materials. Product category and claim wording affect what labels signify.
copy: For a cosmetic with agricultural ingredients, an eligible USDA organic label concerns organic production and handling standards. The label category can depend on the proportion and status of ingredients. That does not tell you whether the finished product produces a particular skin outcome.
Read the stated scope of the label

Read the difference between an organic product claim and a statement about one organic ingredient. Check the certification where it applies, then use separate evidence for performance or tolerance. An ingredient list and a study of the finished formulation answer different questions.
The FDA notes that cosmetic requirements still apply. A label about agricultural sourcing does not replace the other information required for safe and accurate use.
table: Three separate meanings to keep visible
Production and labeling standards under the stated program

article: What does 40 or 80 minutes of water resistance mean on U.S. sunscreen?
Read the FDA’s water-resistance label tests and separate them from the SPF number.
FDA U.S. OTC sunscreen water-resistance labeling guidance. Product directions govern use.
copy: The 40- or 80-minute statement on a U.S. water-resistant sunscreen indicates the tested time for retaining labeled protection under the standardized water exposure. It is a separate claim from the SPF number. The number is not a guarantee for every mix of swimming, sweating and towel drying.
Read the time beside the relevant claim

If a package says water resistant, read the specific duration and the Drug Facts directions. The FDA explains why products cannot claim to be waterproof or sweatproof. A result measured with a set test procedure does not tell you exactly what remains on one person’s skin after any activity.
Use the stated label directions for the specific product. Keep the tested category distinct from everyday conditions.
table: A protection measurement under its test

article: Why can’t the SPF number tell you the whole UVA claim?
Read the FDA tests behind broad spectrum and SPF as two distinct label statements.
U.S. FDA sunscreen labeling and effectiveness testing guidance.
copy: SPF is a measure based on how much UV exposure produces sunburn under test conditions. In U.S. labeling, broad spectrum is a separate test related to protection across ultraviolet wavelengths, including UVA. A larger SPF number alone does not give a separate numeric UVA rating.
Read both parts of the label

The standardized broad-spectrum test uses a wavelength-based threshold. A reader comparing two packages can check for both the SPF and broad-spectrum wording without treating them as interchangeable numbers. A tinted label or a reference to visible light would raise another question that the broad-spectrum claim alone does not answer.
Use the exact package directions and report the market because regulatory labeling can differ across countries.
